Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac (1619–1655) was a real 17th-century French novelist, duelist, and soldier who inspired the famous 1897 play by Edmond Rostand. While the play highlights his large nose and unrequited love for his cousin Roxane, the real Cyrano was equally remarkable as a pioneer of science fiction.

Key Dimensions of His Life

  • The Soldier-Poet: He served in the French Guards and was wounded at the Siege of Arras in 1640. He was renowned for his wit and legendary skill as a swordsman.
  • Science Fiction Pioneer: He wrote The Other World: Comical History of the States and Empires of the Moon (published posthumously), featuring a craft propelled by firecrackers—one of the earliest depictions of space travel.
  • The Free Thinker: A student of the philosopher Pierre Gassendi, Cyrano was a radical "libertine" who questioned the church and explored early atomic theory.

The Legend vs. Reality

FeatureHistorical FactRostand’s Play
The NoseHe did indeed have a prominent nose.It is his defining, tragic physical trait.
RoxaneBased on his cousin, Madeleine Robineau.The romantic object of his secret obsession.
ChristianA fellow soldier who married Madeleine.A handsome but dim soldier Cyrano assists.
DeathDied at 36 after a falling beam hit him.A tragic, poetic death scene in a convent.

Cyrano's Legacy His life embodies "panache"—a word popularized by Rostand’s play to describe flamboyant courage and style. Even today, he remains a symbol of the "outsider" whose intellectual and spiritual depth far exceeds his physical appearance.
